intro: East Hampton is an old village near the eastern end of Long Island, New York. Beside Herrick Park, its green behind Newtown Lane, lie the gardens Douglas Dayton, a former village mayor, planted around his family's house, bought by the town from 2017 as the Douglas E. Dayton Arboretum. A reader walked through it in November and sent us six of its trees, from a royal paulownia to a sourwood and a zelkova in full autumn colour.
meta_description: Six trees of the Douglas E. Dayton Arboretum beside Herrick Park in East Hampton, New York, sent by a reader: a paulownia, a sourwood, a zelkova and more.
question_meta: Six trees in the Dayton Arboretum beside Herrick Park, East Hampton: a beech, a paulownia, a magnolia, a Sawara cypress, a sourwood and a zelkova.
question_answer: The Douglas E. Dayton Arboretum lies beside Herrick Park in East Hampton village, between Pleasant Lane and the park. The town owns the land; check it is open before you go.
question_context: A reader walked through the Douglas E. Dayton Arboretum in East Hampton this November and sent us six of its trees. The arboretum is the old garden of Douglas Dayton, a former mayor of the village, planted around his family's house at the end of Muchmore Lane and on Pleasant Lane, beside Herrick Park. The Town of East Hampton began buying the land in 2017 with community preservation money, the village manages it, and a covenant says it will always carry Dayton's name. In 2022 the village took down a screen of arborvitae between the arboretum and the park, and officials said they wanted the gardens open to the public. Many of the trees carry small black labels with their names. The reader sent a tall royal paulownia, a Sawara cypress with a bench beneath it, an old sourwood with deeply ridged bark, a Japanese zelkova that turns orange beside the car park, a southern magnolia on the edge of the ball fields, and a broad, many-stemmed tree they named a ginkgo, which looks to us like a beech; we would like someone to settle it. We do not yet have measurements or planting dates for any of them.

faq.q: Where are the old trees in East Hampton village?
faq.a: Six of the trees readers have sent us stand in the Douglas E. Dayton Arboretum, beside Herrick Park between Pleasant Lane and the ball fields.

faq.q: Can I visit the Douglas E. Dayton Arboretum?
faq.a: The town owns it and the village manages it. In 2022 it was still fenced while the village worked to open it; a reader walked among the trees in November 2026. Check it is open before you go.

faq.q: When is the best time to see the trees in the Dayton Arboretum?
faq.a: Early November for the zelkova's orange crown and the paulownia going yellow, late spring for the paulownia's violet flowers, and June for the magnolia's white flowers.

trees.story:
The reader who sent us this tree from East Hampton, on the South Fork of Long Island, named it a ginkgo. The photograph shows something else, we think. Smooth, elephant-grey bark, a trunk that flares at the foot into thick roots gripping the lawn, and a vast dome of small oval leaves going copper and gold are how a beech looks in November. Tell us if we have it wrong.

Whatever its name, it is the kind of tree you notice from across a park. The trunk is short and broad and splits low into several great stems that climb together, so the crown is nearly as wide as it is tall and shades a whole stretch of grass. In the reader's picture the ground beneath it is covered in fallen leaves, and a line of other big trees runs off behind it, their dark trunks standing on a bright lawn.

With a second photograph, of the trunk, the reader named it a European beech and puts its girth at about 300 centimetres; those are their figures. We do not know its age. If you have stood under it with a tape, or know the history of this lawn beside Herrick Park, tell us here and we will add your figures.

Walk in under the crown on a sunny autumn afternoon, when the light comes through the turning leaves.

trees.story:
A reader walking the lawns beside Herrick Park in East Hampton sent us this tree, with a second photograph of the black label screwed to its trunk: Royal Paulownia, Paulownia tomentosa. It is the tree also called the empress or princess tree, a native of China named after Anna Pavlovna, the Russian grand duchess who became queen of the Netherlands.

Paulownias are famous for growing fast, and most of the ones planted in gardens stay slim. This one has not. In the reader's picture its pale grey trunk rises thick and straight from the far edge of a mown lawn, the bark broken into the rough, corky plates of an old tree, and the crown climbs well above the dark conifers beside it, its big heart-shaped leaves turning yellow in the November sun. On the other side, a bare tree has already dropped its leaves.

In spring, before the leaves come, a paulownia carries upright sprays of violet flowers shaped like foxgloves, sweetly scented, high in the crown.

We do not know its height, its girth or who planted it. If you know this lawn and its labelled trees, tell us here.

Come in May, when it flowers.

trees.story:
Southern magnolias grow wild on the warm coastal plain of the American South, and Long Island is a long way north of there. A reader sent us this one from East Hampton village, standing alone on open grass beside Herrick Park, with ball fields, a backstop and a goalpost behind it.

Alone is how a magnolia likes to grow. With nothing crowding it, this one has made a broad, full crown on a short dark trunk, every branch thick with big leathery leaves. A second photograph the reader sent shows them close up, longer than a hand, glossy dark green above with the rusty brown felt underneath that gives the species away. In a park where November had stripped the trees around it, it was still in full leaf, because it is evergreen.

In early summer it opens creamy white flowers as big as dinner plates, with a scent people often compare to lemon.

We do not know its age, its girth or who planted it. If you do, tell us here.

Come in June or July for the flowers, or in the middle of winter, when it is the only green crown on the field.

trees.story:
A small black label on this trunk names it: Sawara Cypress, Chamaecyparis pisifera 'Squarrosa'. A reader photographed the label and the tree on a lawn beside Herrick Park in East Hampton, and sent us both.

Sawara cypress comes from the mountains of central and southern Japan. 'Squarrosa' is a garden form, chosen for its soft, feathery, blue-grey foliage, and it is usually planted as a shrub or a small tree at the edge of a border. This one has been left alone long enough to become something else. Its reddish trunk, shedding bark in long fibrous strips, rises thick and straight past a wooden bench and then throws out long crooked limbs that snake sideways and up into a high, open crown. A second big cypress stands just behind it, with the bench between the two, and the lawn runs off under more old trees.

We do not know its age, its height or its girth. If you know who planted the labelled trees on this lawn, or when, tell us here and we will add it.

Sit on the bench between the two trunks and look up into the limbs.

trees.story:
Sourwood is usually a slim, modest tree that grows in the shade of bigger ones, so the reader who sent us this one from East Hampton had a reason to look up. It grows in the Douglas E. Dayton Arboretum, a former mayor's garden of specimen trees beside Herrick Park that the town now owns.

The label on the trunk reads Sourwood, Oxydendrum arboreum, a tree of the eastern United States and the only species in its genus. The reader's photographs show an old one. Its bark has broken into thick blocky ridges, grey and patched with lichen, and the trunk forks into limbs that twist and snake upward against the sky, bare when the reader stood there in November.

In July and August a sourwood hangs out drooping sprays of small white bell-shaped flowers, like lily of the valley, and bees make a prized honey from them. The leaves taste sour, which gave the tree its name, and in autumn they turn scarlet early.

We have no girth or age for this tree yet. If you know them, tell us here.

Come in high summer, when the flowers hang from every branch.

trees.story:
The reader who sent us this tree from East Hampton wrote one word with it: "Size." Their photograph, taken from the car park on a clear November day, makes the point. The crown fills the sky above two parked cars, a great rounded vase of orange and rust and gold, and its fallen leaves have covered the ground and spilled onto the tarmac.

A black label on the trunk names it Japanese zelkova, Zelkova serrata. The species is a relative of the elms from Japan, Korea and China, where the oldest zelkovas are honoured at temples and shrines, and American cities have planted it widely since Dutch elm disease, because it shrugs the disease off. This one grows at the edge of the Douglas E. Dayton Arboretum, the old gardens of a former East Hampton mayor beside Herrick Park, now owned by the town. Up close, its trunk is smooth and grey and peels in small orange patches.

We have no measurement of it yet, only the reader's word for its size. If you have measured it, tell us here.

Come in early November, when the whole crown turns at once.
